analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices and adds a government-run prescription drug plan for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote in either House committee, and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Just after the 2003 Medicare drug law passed, this bill would undo several of its most industry-friendly features. It would repeal the clause that bars the government from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers, and it would have the Secretary of Health and Human Services offer a nationwide public prescription drug plan with a $35 premium, alongside private plans. It would also fully reimburse employers who keep retiree drug coverage, and repeal a fund that subsidized private regional plans and separate cost-containment provisions.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would gain a cheaper government-run drug plan and a government that can negotiate drug prices instead of being barred from doing so. Employers who provide retiree drug coverage would gain full federal reimbursement for doing so.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and employers with retiree plans

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the section of the 2003 Medicare drug law that prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in negotiations between drug manufacturers, pharmacies, and drug plan sponsors, restoring the government's ability to negotiate drug prices [S2] [S3].

It requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer a nationwide prescription drug plan with basic coverage and a $35 premium in 2006, available to every Medicare beneficiary as a choice in addition to private plans [S2] [S3].

It provides full reimbursement for employers' costs of qualified retiree drug coverage and lets those costs count toward seniors' catastrophic limits, encouraging employers to keep retiree benefits [S2] [S3].
It repeals the Comparative Cost Adjustment program and the MA Regional Plan Stabilization Fund, which subsidized private plans created under the 2003 law [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers, whose protection from government price negotiation would end. Private insurers offering Medicare drug plans, who would face a government-run competitor and lose the regional stabilization fund subsidies. Taxpayers, who would fund the new public plan and expanded retiree reimbursements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, private insurers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the cost-containment provisions of the 2003 law and adds a government-run plan plus full retiree reimbursements, all of which would increase federal spending and raise deficit concerns [S2] [S3].

Drug makers argue that government price negotiation reduces revenues available for developing new medicines — an objection their industry made against every negotiation bill of this era (widely reported, not in the provided sources).
Despite its name, the bill does not create universal coverage; it modifies the prescription drug benefit only, so its name overstates what it delivers [S2] [S3].
A public plan priced below private plans could cause private drug plans to exit some markets, concentrating enrollment in a government plan (a structural concern about competing public options).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to seniors — lower drug prices through negotiation and a low-premium public option — are substantial and direct. The main cost is added federal spending, and the design is fairly blunt: it spends more on retiree reimbursements and repeals cost controls without offsetting savings. The bill is modest in scope relative to its name but its core provisions genuinely serve beneficiaries at the expense of drug makers and private plans.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single Democrat with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Cardin (D-MD) introduced the bill on January 20, 2004 [S1] [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees on the day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
It was then referred to the Health Subcommittee of each committee in late January and early February 2004, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, with the bill never reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers kept the ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices, and private insurers kept the drug benefit market without a government-run competitor. Medicare beneficiaries received none of the bill's price protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

for.name: Rep. Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on January 20-21, 2004, but attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on January 23, 2004, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicare financing
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on February 3, 2004, and never considered it further.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee when the bill was referred; the committee never scheduled action on it. He had been a chief architect of the 2003 Medicare drug law the bill sought to amend.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the second committee of referral; the committee never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and the Republican-controlled House committees of referral never acted on it; there were no votes.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 'non-interference' clause from the 2003 Medicare law that bars the government from negotiating drug prices, directly threatening drug revenues on the new Part D benefit. Their interest ran against seniors who would benefit from negotiated prices.

industries.industry: Private health insurers offering Medicare drug and Advantage plans
industries.note: A government-run $35 plan would compete with their products, and the bill repeals the MA Regional Plan Stabilization Fund that subsidized private regional plans. Private plans remain part of the program, but with a public competitor and less federal support.

industries.industry: Large employers with retiree health plans
industries.note: The bill provides full federal reimbursement for employers' costs of qualified retiree drug coverage, making it easier for them to keep offering retiree benefits — which retirees also gain from.
